Elkhart man, 90, picks up the hammer every week as volunteer for Habitat for Humanity (article in comments to avoid ad)

At 90 years old, Chuck Vetter has lent a hand, as well as his hammer, to more than 150 Habitat for Humanity builds in Elkhart County.

Vetter, an Elkhart resident who turned 90 late last year, has been volunteering with Habitat for Humanity of Elkhart County since the local chapter started in 1986.

“I like doing building work and I like the organization and what they do,” he said.

Vetter works on Habitat projects once a week now, scaling back from when he used to work more often following his retirement from the Bendix Corp., where he worked as an engineer.

Molly Prime, the group’s community volunteer coordinator, said Vetter is very handy and can take do numerous homebuilding projects. Despite his age, the nonagenarian still solicits his help as often as she can.

“I call and invite him every week,” Prime said. “He’s good at just about everything.”

While Vetter can do a lot and enjoys it, there are some things he’s stopped doing. “I don’t get up on the roof anymore,” Vetter said.

In honor of Vetter’s 90th birthday, Prime said that the organization had a fundraising campaign asking for donations of $90.90. She said Habitat was able to hit its goal of $9,000, with all the money going toward a home under construction on Bedford Court in Elkhart, where Vetter was working this week.

According to Prime, a typical Habitat project costs about $70,000 to build.

In the 30 years that the county’s Habitat chapter has operated, Prime said that it has constructed around 180 homes and Vetter estimates he’s worked on all but a handful of those homes, mostly missing out on ones that single large groups worked on alone.

Vetter said he is happy to help out those less fortunate than himself. “It’s something I can do and I can contribute a little bit to other people,” he said.

While many people his age like to take it easy, Vetter said staying occupied is important to him.

“I got six days a week to relax,” he said. “I need something to keep me busy and get me out of the house once in a while.”

Despite his age and the number of homes he has worked on, Vetter says there is little chance he will slow down any time soon.

“As long as I can do it, I think I’ll keep plugging away,” he said.
